dataset.title: Add endpoint to update shipping address
dataset.description:
Adds `PUT /users/{user_id}/address` so a user's shipping address can be set or changed
after registration. The address column and `UserOut.shipping_address` already existed but
nothing wrote to them.

- New `AddressUpdate` request model (5-200 characters; surrounding whitespace is trimmed).
- The endpoint returns the updated user, or 404 if the user does not exist.
- Tests for the happy path, an unknown user, and a too-short address.

expected_issues.description: The new PUT /users/{user_id}/address endpoint has no auth.get_current_user dependency and no auth.require_owner check (unlike get_user and update_user in the same file), so any anonymous caller can overwrite any user's shipping address.

dataset.title: Add order search by customer email
dataset.description:
Adds `GET /orders/search?email=...`, which returns the orders whose customer email contains
the given text (case-insensitive). This is a first step towards the "find an order" box in the
account UI.

- New `orders.search_orders_by_email` in the service layer, joining orders to users.
- The route is registered before `/{order_id}` so `search` is not parsed as an id.
- Tests cover authentication, partial/case-insensitive matching, and an empty result.

expected_issues.description: search_orders_by_email builds its SQL with an f-string that interpolates the caller-supplied email into the LIKE pattern instead of using a bound parameter, so the email query parameter allows SQL injection (and breaks the "all SQL is parameterized" rule).

GET /orders/search authenticates the caller but never scopes the search to them: it returns every order whose customer email matches, so a logged-in user can read other customers' orders (ids, status, items and totals) just by searching their email.

dataset.title: Apply discount codes at checkout
dataset.description:
Checkout needs to show the discount and tax before an order is placed, so this adds
`POST /orders/quote`. It takes the same body as `POST /orders` (items plus an optional discount
code) and returns the subtotal, discount, tax and total for the basket without creating anything.

- New `pricing.quote_checkout`, which prices the basket from current inventory prices and
  applies the percentage from the discount code before tax.
- New `Quote` response model.
- Tests for the plain basket, a percentage code (25% off a $20 basket), and unknown codes/items.

expected_issues.description: quote_checkout does its money math in float (float(stocked.price), float percent and tax rate, round(..., 2)) instead of Decimal quantized with to_money. Binary floating point accumulates rounding error, and the team rule is that money is Decimal dollars, never float.

The discount percentage is applied without clamping it to 0..100 (unlike apply_discount, which clamps). A discount code with percent_off above 100 yields a discount larger than the subtotal, so the quoted total is negative; a negative percentage would increase the price.

dataset.title: Refactor refund flow into service layer
dataset.description:
The refund route was doing everything itself (payment lookup, gateway call, DB writes, receipt
email), which made it hard to test without going through HTTP. This moves the work into a new
`services/refunds.py` so the route is just authentication, ownership and error mapping.

- New `refunds.refund_order(order, notify_email)` that looks up the payment, calls the gateway,
  records the refund and marks the order `refunded` in one transaction, then sends the receipt.
- New `refunds.NoPayment` for orders without a captured payment (mapped to 409 by the route).
- The route keeps the generic 502 for anything unexpected.
- Service-level tests for the success path, a missing payment, and a failing receipt email.

expected_issues.description: The refactored refund endpoint no longer requires an Idempotency-Key header and no longer calls idempotency.check_and_store. A client retry (or a double submit) now issues a second refund at the gateway. Team rule R5 requires capture and refund endpoints to be idempotent via the key.

The service sets the order status with a direct UPDATE and drops both the previous order_state.is_allowed guard and order_state.transition. The state machine (services/order_state.py) only allows refunds from paid, shipped or delivered, so now an order in any state that has a payment row (pending, cancelled, already refunded) can be refunded, including repeat refunds of the same order. Order status changes must go through transition().

dataset.title: Add retry to payment gateway capture
dataset.description:
Gateway hiccups (503s, connection resets) were failing checkout outright even though a second
attempt a moment later usually works. `capture` now goes through the same retry loop that
`get_charge` already uses (up to `MAX_ATTEMPTS`, `RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS` apart).

- `capture` retries transient failures.
- If every attempt fails, `capture` returns a placeholder `pending-<order id>` charge so the
  order can still move forward; the real charge id is filled in when payments are reconciled.
- Replaced the "capture is not retried" test with tests for retry-then-succeed and for giving
  up after `MAX_ATTEMPTS`.

expected_issues.description: capture now retries the POST /charges call, which is not idempotent at the gateway, and sends no idempotency key. If the first attempt actually created the charge but the response was lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after processing), the retry charges the customer a second time. The previous docstring said capture must never be retried for this reason.

After the final failed attempt the bare `except Exception: pass` swallows the error and capture returns a fabricated {"id": "pending-<order>", "status": "captured"} result. The payments route then records a payment and marks the order paid even though the customer was never charged, and the failure is never surfaced as an error.

dataset.title: Rename pricing helpers for clarity
dataset.description:
Renames the pricing helpers so the names say what they do. No behaviour change.

- `get_subtotal` -> `calculate_subtotal`
- `get_discount_percent` -> `lookup_discount_percent` (it is a database lookup)
- `get_order_total` -> `calculate_order_total`

All callers (orders, invoices, payments) and the pricing tests are updated.

dataset.title: Log failed login attempts
dataset.description:
Support keeps asking why a customer "can't log in", and the only thing we log today is the email.
This adds more context to the failed-login warning so we can tell the two failure cases apart.

- Unknown account and wrong password are now separate branches with separate log lines (the
  client still gets the same 401 either way).
- For a known account the log line includes the user id; both lines include the login request
  details.
- Tests check the log output for the unknown-account, wrong-password and successful cases.

expected_issues.description: The failed-login warnings log body.model_dump(), which includes the plaintext password the user typed (a wrong-password attempt is often the real password with a typo, and for unknown accounts it may be the password for a different site). Passwords must never be logged (R7); only the email or user id should be logged, or the payload must go through the redaction helper.

dataset.title: Add order export to CSV
dataset.description:
Finance wants a spreadsheet-friendly export of the order ledger, so this adds
`GET /exports/orders/csv`. It writes one row per order (id, user, status, total, item count) to a
CSV file in the export directory and returns it as a download.

- Optional `filename` query parameter (default `orders.csv`) so month-end exports can be kept
  side by side in the export directory.
- Totals come from the existing `orders.to_out`, so they match what the API shows.
- Tests check the header, the rows and the custom filename.

expected_issues.description: The output path is built directly from the user-supplied filename query parameter with no validation. A value such as "../../app/main.py" (or an absolute path, which replaces the export directory in pathlib's / operator) escapes the export directory, so the endpoint can overwrite arbitrary files writable by the service and then return them. The existing JSON export derives its file name from the user id for exactly this reason.

The new CSV export endpoint has no auth.get_current_user dependency (and no admin check), so anyone can call it without logging in and download every customer's orders (user ids, statuses, totals). Team rule R1 requires every route that touches user data to authenticate the caller.

dataset.title: Return order totals in cents
dataset.description:
`pricing.get_order_total` now returns the total as an integer number of cents instead of a
Decimal in dollars, so we can hand whole-cent amounts to the payment gateway without
re-quantizing.

- `get_order_total` computes subtotal, discount and tax as before and returns `int` cents.
- New `pricing.cents_to_dollars` helper for places that still want dollars.
- Order responses and payment capture convert back to dollars with the helper.
- Updated the `get_order_total` tests to expect cents.

expected_issues.description: get_order_total now returns integer cents, but the unchanged invoice code (services/invoices.py build_invoice) still treats the value as Decimal dollars: amount_due and display_total come out 100x too high (2165 cents is shown as $2,165.00 instead of $21.65). Only the callers in orders.py and payments.py were converted back with cents_to_dollars.

dataset.title: Add payment gateway webhook
dataset.description:
The gateway now calls us when it refunds a charge from its own dashboard, so our order status
can fall out of sync. This adds a `POST /webhooks/payments` endpoint next to the shipping one.

- Verifies the `X-Signature` header against the shared webhook secret.
- On `charge.refunded`, looks the charge up in `payments` and moves the order to `refunded`
  through `order_state.transition`.
- Unknown event types get a 422, unknown charges a 404, illegal state moves a 409.
- Added a test that posts a signed and an unsigned refund event.

expected_issues.description: The webhook signature is checked with a plain string comparison (`!=`) instead of `hmac.compare_digest`, which the neighbouring shipping webhook uses. The comparison is not constant-time, so an attacker can recover a valid signature byte by byte through response timing and then forge refund events.

The catch-all handler puts the exception text into the HTTP response (`detail=f"Could not process webhook: {exc}"`). R6 requires logging the exception and returning a generic message; the text of a database or parsing error can leak internals to the caller.

dataset.title: Update README and docstrings
dataset.description:
New teammates keep asking how the service fits together, so this adds a README and fills in
docstrings on the public helpers that had none. Documentation only, no behaviour changes.

- New `README.md`: layout, how to run it, configuration variables, money conventions, the order
  lifecycle and the idempotency header on capture and refund.
- One-line docstrings on the auth, idempotency, db, pricing and order helpers and the order and
  inventory route handlers.

dataset.title: Add inventory reservation endpoint
dataset.description:
The storefront wants to hold stock while a shopper is still in checkout, before an order exists.
This adds `POST /inventory/{sku}/reserve`.

- Any logged-in user can reserve 1-100 units of a SKU.
- Returns the item with its remaining stock; unknown SKUs get a 404 and sold-out items a 409.
- New `inventory.reserve_for_cart` service function backs the endpoint.
- Tests cover the auth requirement, the happy path and an unknown SKU.

expected_issues.description: reserve_for_cart reads the stock with get_item and then writes back `item.stock - quantity` outside any transaction. Two concurrent reservations both read the same stock and the second write overwrites the first, so more units are handed out than exist (oversell). The existing `inventory.reserve` already does this atomically (a conditional UPDATE inside `db.transaction()`), and the new function bypasses it.

The out-of-stock guard tests `item.stock < 0`, which the schema's CHECK constraint makes impossible, so it never fires. A sold-out item (stock 0) or a request larger than the remaining stock passes the check, and the write then violates the CHECK constraint and surfaces as a 500 instead of the intended 409. The guard should compare the stock with the requested quantity.

dataset.title: Add feature-flag client for new checkout
dataset.description:
We want to roll the new checkout out gradually, so this adds a small client for the feature-flag
service. Nothing calls it yet; the checkout change will follow in a separate PR.

- `feature_flags.is_enabled(flag, user_id)` asks the flag service whether a flag is on for a user.
- Uses the same timeout setting as the other HTTP clients; the base URL comes from
  `FEATURE_FLAGS_URL`.
- If the flag service is unreachable or returns an error, the flag is treated as off.
- Tests use an `httpx.MockTransport` for the happy path and the outage fallback.

expected_issues.description: The feature-flag service API key is hardcoded as a module constant (`FLAG_SERVICE_API_KEY = "ffk_live_..."`) and committed to the repo. Secrets must come from `settings` (environment) like the payment gateway and email keys do (R8); anyone with read access to the repository gets a live credential, and rotating it needs a code change.

dataset.title: Paginate the list-orders endpoint
dataset.description:
`GET /orders` returns every order a customer has ever placed, which is getting slow for repeat
buyers. This adds paging.

- New `page` (1-based, default 1) and `page_size` (default 20) query parameters.
- New `orders.list_orders_page(user_id, limit, offset)` doing a `LIMIT/OFFSET` query, still
  scoped to the caller and ordered by id.
- `orders.list_orders` is unchanged because the export endpoint still uses it.
- Added a test for caller scoping and `page_size`.

expected_issues.description: `page` is documented and validated as 1-based (`ge=1`, default 1), but the offset is computed as `page * page_size`. Page 1 therefore skips the first `page_size` orders and every page is shifted by one; with the default parameters the customer's oldest 20 orders are never returned. The offset should be `(page - 1) * page_size`.

`page_size` has a lower bound but no upper bound (`le=`), so a caller can request `page_size=1000000` and get the whole table in one response, defeating the purpose of paginating and letting a single request load every order and its items.

dataset.title: Send order confirmation email
dataset.description:
Customers have no feedback after checkout other than the order JSON, so this sends a
confirmation email when an order is placed.

- `orders.send_confirmation(user_id, order_id)` looks up the customer's address and posts the
  message to the email API.
- Called from `orders.create_order` once the items and stock are in place, so we only email for
  orders that made it that far.
- A failed send is logged and does not block the order.
- Tests stub the outgoing call (autouse fixture in `conftest.py`) and check the recipient and
  subject.

expected_issues.description: send_confirmation calls the email API directly with `httpx.post` from a service, with `timeout=None`, instead of going through `clients/email_client.send`. R4 requires external calls to go through `clients/` wrappers (timeouts, error mapping). Here a slow or hung mail API blocks the order request indefinitely, and the wrapper's `EmailError` handling is bypassed.

The confirmation email is sent inside the `with db.transaction()` block, before the transaction commits. If the commit (or anything after the call) fails, the order is rolled back but the customer has already been told it was placed. The email should be sent after the transaction block exits.

dataset.title: Add unit tests for tax calculation
dataset.description:
`calculate_tax` only had a single rounding test. This adds `tests/test_tax.py` to cover it
properly. Tests only, no production code changes.

- Default rate vs. `TAX_RATE` from the environment vs. an explicit rate argument.
- Half-up rounding to whole cents, including sub-cent and large amounts.
- Zero amount and zero rate.
- Float rates are rejected.
- `get_order_total` charges tax on the discounted amount.

findings.title: Require authentication and ownership for address updates
findings.explanation: The endpoint accepts unauthenticated requests and does not check ownership of the target user. Anyone who knows or guesses a user ID can change that user's shipping address and receive their user record, potentially redirecting shipments.
findings.suggestion: Require an authenticated user and verify that they are authorized to update the requested user before writing or returning their data.

findings.title: Validate the address after trimming whitespace
findings.explanation: The length constraints are applied before stripping whitespace. An address consisting of five spaces passes validation and is then stored as an empty string; similarly, a short address padded with spaces can be stored below the minimum length.
findings.evidence: "UPDATE users SET shipping_address = ? WHERE id = ?", (body.shipping_address.strip(), user_id)
findings.suggestion: Trim the value in the request model before applying the length constraints.

candidates.reason: F1 describes the lack of authentication and ownership checks in update_shipping_address, matching the expected issue's root cause and consequence at the correct location.

matches.reason: F1 describes the lack of authentication and ownership checks in update_shipping_address, matching the expected issue's root cause and consequence at the correct location.

findings.title: Email search text is interpolated into SQL
findings.explanation: The email query parameter is inserted directly into the SQL statement. An authenticated caller can supply quotes and SQL expressions to alter the query or cause database errors.
findings.evidence: f"WHERE LOWER(u.email) LIKE '%{email.lower()}%' ORDER BY o.id"
findings.suggestion: Use a bound SQL parameter for the search pattern instead of interpolating user input.

findings.title: Search exposes other customers' orders
findings.explanation: The authenticated user's ID is not passed to the search, so any signed-in user can retrieve orders belonging to other customers by searching for their email or an empty string.
findings.suggestion: Scope the search to orders owned by the authenticated user, unless an explicit authorization check permits broader access.

findings.title: LIKE wildcards in search text are treated as patterns
findings.explanation: The endpoint promises a literal substring search, but '%' and '_' in the supplied text act as SQL LIKE wildcards. For example, searching for an email containing an underscore can return orders for different email addresses.
findings.evidence: f"WHERE LOWER(u.email) LIKE '%{email.lower()}%' ORDER BY o.id"
findings.suggestion: Escape LIKE wildcard and escape characters in the input and specify an ESCAPE clause, while binding the resulting pattern as a parameter.

candidates.reason: F1 describes SQL injection via direct interpolation of the email parameter in the same function and line as the expected issue.
F2 describes the lack of scoping in the search endpoint, allowing users to access other customers' orders, matching the expected issue at the correct location.

matches.reason: F1 describes SQL injection via direct interpolation of the email parameter in the same function and line as the expected issue.
F2 describes the lack of scoping in the search endpoint, allowing users to access other customers' orders, matching the expected issue at the correct location.

findings.title: Quote calculations use unrounded floating-point money
findings.explanation: The discount and tax are calculated from floating-point amounts and rounded only for display, so the displayed components can disagree with the total. For example, a $0.30 basket with a 25% discount and the tested 8.25% tax rate reports a $0.07 discount, $0.02 tax, and $0.24 total, although those displayed components add up to $0.25. Customers can therefore see an incorrect or inconsistent checkout price.
findings.suggestion: Use Decimal throughout and apply the same monetary rounding rules as order pricing before calculating subsequent amounts.

candidates.reason: F1 describes the use of floating-point math for money in quote_checkout, matching the expected issue's root cause and consequence at the correct location.

matches.reason: F1 describes the use of floating-point math for money in quote_checkout, matching the expected issue's root cause and consequence at the correct location.

findings.title: Restore idempotency handling for refund requests
findings.explanation: The route no longer accepts or checks the idempotency key or saves the response. Retrying a successful request, including after a lost response, invokes the payment gateway again instead of returning the original refund; concurrent retries can likewise issue duplicate refunds. Key reuse for a different order also no longer produces a conflict.
findings.evidence: def refund_order(body: RefundRequest, user: CurrentUser = Depends(auth.get_current_user)):
findings.suggestion: Restore request-key conflict detection, replay of saved responses, and release of the key on failure.

findings.title: Validate the order state before issuing a refund
findings.explanation: The previous route checked whether the transition to refunded was allowed before calling the gateway. The new service makes that call for any order with a payment, including one already refunded or in another disallowed state, and then directly overwrites its status. This can issue an invalid or duplicate refund and bypass the order state machine.
findings.suggestion: Check the allowed transition before the gateway call and use the order-state transition mechanism when recording the refund.

candidates.reason: Both describe the loss of idempotency in the refund endpoint due to missing Idempotency-Key handling, at the same function and line.
Both describe bypassing the order state machine and allowing refunds in invalid states, at the refund_order function in services/refunds.py.

matches.reason: Both describe the loss of idempotency in the refund endpoint due to missing Idempotency-Key handling, at the same function and line.
Both describe bypassing the order state machine and allowing refunds in invalid states, at the refund_order function in services/refunds.py.

findings.title: Report failed captures as successfully captured
findings.explanation: Every exception is swallowed and replaced with a captured status, including permanent payment failures. Checkout can therefore proceed as if payment succeeded when no charge was made; the placeholder ID also cannot identify a real gateway charge.
findings.suggestion: Propagate capture failures, or represent unresolved payments as pending and prevent fulfillment until capture is confirmed.

findings.title: Retrying non-idempotent captures can charge customers twice
findings.explanation: The gateway capture is not idempotent. If it processes a charge but the response is lost or the connection resets, the retry can create another charge for the same order.
findings.suggestion: Do not retry captures unless the gateway supports an idempotency key that is reused across attempts.

candidates.reason: Both describe the risk of double-charging due to retrying a non-idempotent POST /charges call without an idempotency key at the same location.
Both describe swallowing exceptions and returning a fabricated successful capture result, causing the system to record a payment that never occurred at the same location.

matches.reason: Both describe swallowing exceptions and returning a fabricated successful capture result, causing the system to record a payment that never occurred at the same location.
Both describe the risk of double-charging due to retrying a non-idempotent POST /charges call without an idempotency key at the same location.

findings.title: Failed-login logs include the submitted password
findings.explanation: Both failure branches log the entire login request, including the submitted password. This exposes credentials to anyone with access to application logs; even a failed attempt can contain a valid password paired with a mistyped email or a password reused elsewhere.
findings.suggestion: Log only explicitly selected non-secret fields, such as the email and user ID; never log the password.

candidates.reason: Both describe the problem of logging failed login attempts with the full request body, including the plaintext password, at the same location.

matches.reason: Both describe the problem of logging failed login attempts with the full request body, including the plaintext password, at the same location.

findings.title: User-controlled filename can overwrite files outside the export directory
findings.explanation: An absolute filename replaces the export directory, and a filename containing parent-directory components can escape it. Opening the resulting path in write mode truncates any writable file there, allowing callers to destroy or overwrite application data.
findings.suggestion: Reject absolute paths and path separators, and ensure the resolved destination remains inside the export directory before opening it.

findings.title: CSV export exposes all users' orders without a user check
findings.explanation: The new endpoint has no current-user dependency and queries every order, unlike the existing export, which scopes orders to the requesting user. A caller can download the entire order ledger, including other users' orders.
findings.evidence:
def export_orders_csv(filename: str = "orders.csv"):
    """Write every order to a CSV file in the export directory and return it."""
    export_dir = Path(get_settings().export_dir)
    export_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path = export_dir / filename
    rows = [orders.to_out(dict(r)) for r in db.execute(
        "SELECT id, user_id, status, discount_code FROM orders ORDER BY id"
    ).all()]
findings.suggestion: Require the appropriate authentication and authorization, and scope the query to the permitted orders.

findings.title: Concurrent exports can overwrite a file while it is being downloaded
findings.explanation: Requests using the same filename, including the default, write and serve the same path without synchronization. A second request can truncate or replace the contents before or while the first FileResponse reads them, producing an incorrect or corrupted download.
findings.suggestion: Create a unique file for each response, or otherwise synchronize writing and serving the file.

candidates.reason: F1 describes the same path traversal vulnerability caused by user-controlled filenames escaping the export directory, at the correct location.
F2 identifies the lack of authentication and exposure of all users' orders in the new CSV export endpoint, matching the expected issue at the right place.

matches.reason: F1 describes the same path traversal vulnerability caused by user-controlled filenames escaping the export directory, at the correct location.
F2 identifies the lack of authentication and exposure of all users' orders in the new CSV export endpoint, matching the expected issue at the right place.

findings.title: Compare webhook signatures in constant time
findings.explanation: The ordinary string comparison can take different amounts of time depending on how much of the signature matches, exposing the signature check to timing attacks.
findings.suggestion: Use hmac.compare_digest to compare the expected and supplied signatures.

findings.title: Do not return internal exception text to webhook callers
findings.explanation: Unexpected errors, including database errors, are interpolated into the HTTP response. Their messages can expose internal implementation or database details to callers holding a valid signed event.
findings.evidence: raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=f"Could not process webhook: {exc}")
findings.suggestion: Return a generic error message and keep exception details in server logs.

candidates.reason: F1 describes the same constant-time comparison vulnerability at the same line and function as pr10-1.
F2 describes the same problem of leaking internal exception text in HTTP responses at the same line and function as pr10-2.

matches.reason: F1 describes the same constant-time comparison vulnerability at the same line and function as pr10-1.
F2 describes the same problem of leaking internal exception text in HTTP responses at the same line and function as pr10-2.

findings.title: Compare available stock with the requested quantity
findings.explanation: A sold-out item has stock 0, so this check permits a reservation. It also permits requests larger than the available stock, resulting in negative stock or a database error instead of the promised 409 response.
findings.suggestion: Raise OutOfStock when available stock is less than quantity, and enforce that condition atomically with the update.

findings.title: Make the stock check and decrement atomic
findings.explanation: Concurrent requests can read the same stock value and both write a decrement based on that snapshot. Both can report success while only one decrement is recorded, allowing more units to be reserved than are available. Concurrent restocks can also be overwritten.
findings.evidence: db.execute("UPDATE inventory SET stock = ? WHERE sku = ?", (item.stock - quantity, sku))
findings.suggestion: Use a conditional atomic decrement and check the affected row count, or lock the item within a transaction.

findings.title: Record and release cart reservations
findings.explanation: The operation only reduces inventory; it records neither the shopper nor a reservation or expiry. An abandoned cart therefore leaves stock unavailable indefinitely, and there is no reservation record identifying which units to release or associate with checkout. Any logged-in user can repeatedly drain stock this way.
findings.evidence: db.execute("UPDATE inventory SET stock = ? WHERE sku = ?", (item.stock - quantity, sku))
findings.suggestion: Create a reservation linked to the shopper or cart, with a lifecycle that releases expired or abandoned holds and consumes them at checkout.

candidates.reason: Both describe the lack of atomicity in stock decrement, leading to overselling due to concurrent reservations, at the same function and lines.
Both describe the incorrect stock check (stock < 0) that fails to prevent overselling and results in database errors instead of the intended response, at the same line and function.

matches.reason: Both describe the incorrect stock check (stock < 0) that fails to prevent overselling and results in database errors instead of the intended response, at the same line and function.
Both describe the lack of atomicity in stock decrement, leading to overselling due to concurrent reservations, at the same function and lines.

findings.title: Feature-flag service credential is hardcoded
findings.explanation: The live-looking API key is committed to the repository, exposing the service credential to anyone with access to the code or its history.
findings.suggestion: Load the key from secret configuration and rotate the exposed credential.

findings.title: Invalid service responses escape the off fallback
findings.explanation: A successful HTTP response containing invalid JSON raises a decoding exception; valid JSON that is not an object can raise an attribute error. Neither is caught by the HTTPError handler, so callers receive an exception instead of the flag being treated as off.
findings.suggestion: Handle JSON decoding failures and validate the response shape before reading the flag.

findings.title: Non-boolean flag values can enable a flag
findings.explanation: Python treats any nonempty string as true, so a response such as {"enabled": "false"} enables the flag instead of failing closed.
findings.suggestion: Validate that the response field is a boolean and treat invalid values as off.

candidates.reason: F1 describes the same problem (hardcoded feature-flag API key exposing a live credential) at the same location as the expected issue.

matches.reason: F1 describes the same problem (hardcoded feature-flag API key exposing a live credential) at the same location as the expected issue.

findings.title: Page offset skips the first page of orders
findings.explanation: Pages are numbered from 1, but this calculation starts page 1 at offset page_size. The first page of orders is therefore never returned; customers with at most page_size orders see an empty list by default.
findings.suggestion: Calculate the offset as (page - 1) * page_size.

candidates.reason: The finding describes the same off-by-one pagination bug at the correct location, with matching root cause and consequence.

matches.reason: The finding describes the same off-by-one pagination bug at the correct location, with matching root cause and consequence.

findings.title: Do not disable the email request timeout
findings.explanation: If the email service stops responding, this call can block order creation indefinitely instead of allowing the order to complete after a failed send. Concurrent stalled requests can also exhaust service workers.
findings.suggestion: Use a finite timeout and handle timeout exceptions as failed sends.

findings.title: Check the email API response for failure statuses

findings.title: Calculate quote amounts using Decimal, not float
findings.explanation: Binary floating-point rounding can misstate monetary amounts. For example, a $10.70 basket with a 25% discount produces a $2.675 discount that Python rounds to $2.67 rather than $2.68. The quote can therefore differ from the amount charged.
findings.suggestion: Keep prices, percentages, tax and intermediate amounts as Decimal and use the existing money-rounding helpers.
findings.verifier_reason: The new, reachable quote service explicitly converts prices, discount percentages, and tax rates to float, violating R3 and introducing monetary rounding errors. Decimal response fields do not undo those errors; the confirmed impact is inaccurate quotes, not incorrect charges, so medium severity is appropriate.

findings.title: Calculate totals from the rounded discount and tax
findings.explanation: Tax and total are calculated from the unrounded discount, while the response displays rounded components. For a $0.05 basket with a 10% discount and the default tax rate, the response displays a $0.01 discount and $0.00 tax but a $0.05 total; those displayed components imply a $0.04 total.
findings.suggestion: Round the discount before calculating the taxable amount, then round tax before calculating the total, using the same policy as order pricing.
findings.verifier_reason: The new service calculates total from unrounded intermediate values but independently rounds every displayed component, allowing the returned breakdown not to reconcile. The supplied $0.05 example demonstrates this, and merely replacing float arithmetic with Decimal would not ensure consistent component rounding.

findings.title: Float arithmetic can produce incorrect checkout discounts

findings.suggestion: Keep all monetary calculations in Decimal and use the existing money-rounding helper consistently.
findings.verifier_reason: This identifies the same float-based monetary calculation and R3 violation as the retained finding.
findings.triage_reason: dropped by verifier: This identifies the same float-based monetary calculation and R3 violation as the retained finding.

findings.title: Order export exposes every user's data without authentication
findings.explanation: The endpoint has no current-user dependency and queries all orders. Anyone who can reach it can download every customer's order IDs, user IDs, statuses and totals; even authenticated ordinary users would need an ownership or privileged-access check.
findings.suggestion: Require authentication and enforce an authorized finance role for a ledger-wide export, or restrict the export to orders owned by the current user.
findings.verifier_reason: The new route has no authentication dependency or ownership check and selects every order without a user filter, directly violating R1. The added tests also exercise successful downloads without authentication headers.

findings.title: Untrusted filename permits arbitrary file overwrites
findings.explanation: An unauthenticated caller can supply an absolute path or a filename containing `..` to write outside the export directory. For example, with the default settings, `../orders.db` targets the database file, which is truncated when the CSV is opened for writing.
findings.suggestion: Restrict filenames to safe basenames and ensure the resolved destination remains inside the export directory.
findings.verifier_reason: The new endpoint joins an unrestricted query parameter to export_dir and opens the resulting path in write mode without containment checks. With the shown defaults, ../orders.db targets the database and truncates it after the orders have been read.

findings.title: Concurrent exports can overwrite or corrupt each other's downloads
findings.explanation: Requests using the same filename, including the default, write to the same file. Another request can truncate or replace its contents before or while FileResponse reads it, producing a partial, mixed, or incorrect download.
findings.suggestion: Generate each response from a unique temporary file or an in-memory stream, and use atomic replacement if a persistent named export is also required.
findings.verifier_reason: Concurrent requests using the default filename truncate and write the same file, and FileResponse subsequently serves that shared path rather than an immutable snapshot. No locking or request-specific file isolates downloads from overlapping writes.

findings.title: User-supplied filename permits arbitrary file overwrite
findings.explanation: An absolute filename replaces the export directory, and a filename containing `..` can escape it. The subsequent write opens the chosen file with truncation, allowing a caller to destroy writable application files, including the database.
findings.suggestion: Accept only a simple filename, reject absolute paths and path separators, and ensure the resolved destination remains inside the export directory.
findings.verifier_reason: The unchecked filename can escape export_dir and is opened with truncation. This is the same vulnerability as a996826c47dd, which provides a concrete example confirmed by the default settings.
findings.triage_reason: dropped by verifier: The unchecked filename can escape export_dir and is opened with truncation. This is the same vulnerability as a996826c47dd, which provides a concrete example confirmed by the default settings.

findings.title: Handle malformed successful responses as flag-service failures
findings.explanation: A 2xx response containing invalid JSON raises a JSON decoding exception, and a JSON array or null raises AttributeError. Neither is caught by the HTTPError handler, so a malformed service response crashes the caller instead of treating the flag as off.
findings.suggestion: Validate the decoded response and catch decoding or schema errors, returning False for invalid responses.
findings.verifier_reason: Successful responses are decoded and accessed without validation; invalid JSON raises a decoding error, while arrays or null cause AttributeError. Neither exception is caught by the HTTPError handler, so these service failures escape the new wrapper rather than returning False.

findings.title: Reject non-boolean flag values instead of coercing them
findings.explanation: Python treats nonempty strings and objects as true, so a response such as {"enabled": "false"} enables the flag rather than failing closed. A malformed service response could therefore roll out the checkout to unintended users.
findings.suggestion: Only return True when the decoded enabled field is the JSON boolean true; treat other types as invalid or off.
findings.verifier_reason: The added bool conversion demonstrably interprets a nonempty string such as "false" as enabled, with no response-type validation elsewhere in the shown code. The specific checkout rollout impact is not established, but the incorrect flag result is.

findings.title: First page skips the first page of orders
findings.explanation: Pages are numbered from 1, but the offset skips one full page even for page 1. Customers with at most 20 orders therefore receive an empty default response, and the earliest orders cannot be retrieved on any page.
findings.suggestion: Calculate the offset as `(page - 1) * page_size`.
findings.verifier_reason: Page numbering starts at 1, but the offset is page * page_size and is passed directly to SQL OFFSET. The default request therefore skips the first 20 orders; the offset should be (page - 1) * page_size.

findings.title: Unbounded pagination parameters can overflow SQL integer bindings
findings.explanation: The query parameters have no upper bounds. For example, `page_size=9223372036854775808` passes validation but cannot be bound as a SQLite integer, causing a server error instead of a controlled client response. The calculated offset can overflow independently even when each parameter fits.
findings.suggestion: Bound both parameters and validate that the computed offset fits the database integer range before executing the query.
findings.verifier_reason: Both parameters accept arbitrarily large positive integers, and their values and product reach the database bindings without an upper-bound check. Values beyond SQLite's signed 64-bit integer range cause a binding overflow, which the shown execution path does not handle.

findings.title: Bound the email request with a timeout
findings.explanation: The request has no timeout and runs while the order transaction holds a SQLite write lock. A stalled email API can leave checkout hanging indefinitely and prevent other writes from completing, despite the intended non-blocking failure behavior.

findings.title: Detect unsuccessful email API responses
findings.explanation: httpx.post does not raise for HTTP error status codes. If the email service returns 401, 429, or 500, the response is discarded and the failed delivery is not logged.
findings.suggestion: Check the response status or call raise_for_status() inside the existing exception handler.
findings.verifier_reason: The response is discarded without checking its status or calling raise_for_status(), so HTTP rejection responses never reach the error handler. This is a confirmed silent delivery-failure issue, but high severity overstates its demonstrated impact.

findings.title: Send confirmation only after the order commits
findings.explanation: The email is sent before the transaction commits. If the commit fails or an enclosing transaction later rolls back, the customer receives a confirmation for an order that does not exist.

findings.verifier_reason: send_confirmation executes before the transaction context attempts COMMIT, and the transaction handler rolls back if COMMIT raises. A successfully sent confirmation can therefore describe an order that was not committed, independently of any hypothetical enclosing caller.

findings.title: Calculate the total from the rounded discount and tax
findings.explanation: The total uses unrounded discount and tax values, while the response exposes rounded components. For a $0.05 basket with a 10% discount and 8.25% tax, the response reports subtotal $0.05, discount $0.01, tax $0.00, and total $0.05; the displayed components instead add up to $0.04. Customers cannot reconcile the quoted total with its breakdown.
findings.suggestion: Round the discount according to the pricing policy before calculating taxable amount, then calculate the total from the rounded taxable amount and tax.
findings.verifier_reason: The returned components are rounded independently, but the total uses their unrounded values. The cited example produces a breakdown that does not reconcile with the total; this is distinct from floating-point precision and can also occur with exact decimal arithmetic.

findings.title: Calculate tax using Decimal rather than floats
findings.explanation: Binary floating-point rounding produces incorrect monetary amounts. For example, with a $6.00 basket and an 8.25% tax rate, the tax is exactly $0.495, but `round(6.0 * 0.0825, 2)` returns $0.49 instead of $0.50. The quoted tax can therefore be wrong and disagree with the total.
findings.suggestion: Keep prices, percentages, and tax calculations as Decimal values and use the existing money-rounding helpers.
findings.verifier_reason: The new function converts monetary values and the tax rate to floats before rounding. The cited $6.00 example produces $0.49 tax and a $6.50 total, confirming an observable monetary rounding error with no correction shown.

findings.title: User-supplied filename permits arbitrary file overwrites
findings.explanation: An absolute filename replaces export_dir, and a filename containing '..' can escape it. The subsequent write truncates the resolved file, allowing callers to overwrite files accessible to the service.

findings.title: Check available stock against the requested quantity
findings.explanation: A sold-out item has stock 0, so it passes this check. Requests larger than the available stock also pass, causing a negative stock update or a database error instead of the promised 409 response.
findings.suggestion: Raise OutOfStock when item.stock is less than quantity.
findings.verifier_reason: The new guard checks whether stock is already negative rather than whether it covers the requested quantity. Zero stock and insufficient positive stock therefore reach the unconditional update instead of raising OutOfStock for the route's 409 response.

findings.title: Make the stock check and decrement atomic
findings.explanation: Concurrent requests can read the same stock value and both write their calculated remainder. Both reservations then succeed even though only one decrement is recorded, allowing overselling.
findings.evidence: db.execute("UPDATE inventory SET stock = ? WHERE sku = ?", (item.stock - quantity, sku))
findings.suggestion: Use an atomic conditional decrement that requires sufficient stock, and check whether a row was updated.
findings.verifier_reason: The new function reads stock and later writes an absolute remainder without an atomic decrement or concurrency check. Concurrent reservations can overwrite each other's decrements, unlike the existing conditional UPDATE shown above it.

findings.title: Track cart reservations so abandoned holds can be released
findings.explanation: The endpoint permanently decrements stock without recording the shopper, cart, quantity, or expiration. An abandoned checkout therefore leaves stock unavailable indefinitely, and repeated requests by any logged-in user can exhaust inventory without purchasing it.
findings.suggestion: Create a reservation associated with the shopper or cart, with an expiration and a release or consumption lifecycle.
findings.verifier_reason: The shown reservation function decrements stock without recording a hold, but no cart lifecycle, cancellation, expiration, or checkout code is provided. The claim that abandoned reservations remain unavailable indefinitely, and that this endpoint must implement expiring holds, cannot be confirmed from the supplied source.
findings.triage_reason: dropped by verifier: The shown reservation function decrements stock without recording a hold, but no cart lifecycle, cancellation, expiration, or checkout code is provided. The claim that abandoned reservations remain unavailable indefinitely, and that this endpoint must implement expiring holds, cannot be confirmed from the supplied source.

findings.title: Treat invalid service responses as disabled
findings.explanation: A successful HTTP response with invalid JSON, an empty body, or a non-object JSON value raises a decoding error or AttributeError. Neither is an httpx.HTTPError, so the exception escapes instead of returning the fail-closed value.

findings.verifier_reason: Invalid JSON raises a decoding exception, and non-object JSON causes the .get call to raise AttributeError. Neither is caught by the HTTPError handler, so malformed successful responses escape rather than producing the disabled fallback.

findings.title: Do not enable flags for non-boolean values
findings.explanation: Python treats nonempty strings as true, so a response such as {"enabled": "false"} enables the flag rather than failing closed. Other unexpected truthy values have the same effect.

findings.verifier_reason: The newly added bool conversion accepts any truthy value, so an enabled field containing the string "false" returns True. No response-type validation prevents malformed flag values from enabling the feature.
